```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.2, out.width = "100%", dpi = 110)
options(digits = 4)
```

Decay and lag (how many periods carryover may span, the `max_lag` argument)
have to come from somewhere. Priors and vendor benchmarks are one answer.
Cross-validation is another, and it has the advantage of being checkable: if
the procedure works, it should recover a decay you planted in simulated data.

This vignette is about cross-validating carryover correctly, because there is
a tempting way to do it that does not work.

```{r}
library(mediamix)
```

## The objective that does not work

Here is a plausible-sounding procedure. Adstock the media series, fit a linear
trend to the transformed series, extrapolate it one period ahead, and score it
against the raw series. Grid-search decay and lag; take the best.

It sounds reasonable, but there is no dependent variable anywhere in that
loop. The criterion never sees the KPI. It scores how well a trend through the
transformed media forecasts the raw media, which is a property of the filter,
not evidence about the media.

Watch what it does on data where the true decay is 0.7:

```{r}
set.seed(42)
n <- 156
spend <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, 500, 250))
truth <- 0.7
kpi <- 200 + 0.5 * adstock_geometric(spend, decay = truth) + rnorm(n, sd = 5)

no_kpi_objective <- function(x, max_lag, decay) {
  z <- adstock_geometric(x, decay, max_lag = max_lag)
  errs <- vapply(78:(n - 1), function(e) {
    m <- lm(z[1:e] ~ seq_len(e))
    (x[e + 1] - (coef(m)[1] + coef(m)[2] * (e + 1)))^2
  }, numeric(1))
  sqrt(mean(errs))
}

g <- expand.grid(max_lag = c(2, 5, 10, 20), decay = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
g$error <- mapply(function(l, d) no_kpi_objective(spend, l, d),
                  g$max_lag, g$decay)
g[order(g$error), ]
```

Two things are wrong here. The chosen decay is `r g$decay[which.min(g$error)]`
against a truth of 0.7. And look at how little separates the contenders:

```{r}
spread <- c(spread_across_whole_grid = max(g$error) / min(g$error) - 1,
            spread_across_best_four = sort(g$error)[4] / min(g$error) - 1)
spread
```

The four best cells are within
`r signif(100 * spread[["spread_across_best_four"]], 1)`% of one another, and
the whole grid spans `r round(100 * spread[["spread_across_whole_grid"]], 1)`%.
There is almost no signal to select on, and what signal there is runs in a
single direction: error rises monotonically with decay, because a
harder-smoothed series is a worse predictor of a noisy raw one. The criterion
is ranking filters by how much they smooth. It never sees the KPI, so it
cannot rank them by anything else.

## Putting the KPI in the loop

`tune_carryover()` scores each candidate `(max_lag, decay)` by how well a model
fitted on the adstocked media predicts *held-out KPI*. By default the model is
`fit_ols()`, a least-squares regression of the KPI on the adstocked media, and
the resampling is rolling-origin: fit on the first half of the series, forecast
the next period, add that period to the training set and repeat.

```{r}
tuned <- tune_carryover(
  spend, kpi,
  max_lags = Inf,
  decays = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)
)
tuned
```

The printout gives the number of splits and grid points, the selected decay
with its half-life, and the cross-validated error of the winner: the root mean
squared error of all `r tuned$n_splits` one-period forecasts, with its standard
error. The selected decay, `r tuned$best$decay`, is the true one. The profile of
that error across the decay grid shows how sharply the data identifies it:

```{r}
plot(tuned, truth = truth)
```

A clear valley at the truth is what a well-identified carryover looks like.
And it is not a fluke of one decay value:

```{r}
recover <- function(true_decay, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  x <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, 500, 250))
  y <- 200 + 0.5 * adstock_geometric(x, decay = true_decay) + rnorm(n, sd = 5)
  t <- suppressWarnings(tune_carryover(
    x, y, max_lags = Inf, decays = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)))
  c(true = true_decay, recovered = t$best$decay,
    true_hl = half_life(true_decay), recovered_hl = t$best$half_life)
}

round(t(vapply(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.7, 0.85), recover, numeric(4))), 3)
```

A recovery test of this kind, on other simulated series, runs in the
package's own test suite. It is the check that the objective is measuring what
it claims to.

## Why slicing a fully adstocked series is legitimate

`tune_carryover()` adstocks the whole series once per grid point and then cuts
it into folds, rather than re-adstocking inside each fold. That looks like
leakage and is not, because the filter is strictly causal:

```{r}
z <- adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.7)
all.equal(z[1:40], adstock_geometric(spend[1:40], decay = 0.7))
all.equal(z[1:100], adstock_geometric(spend[1:100], decay = 0.7))
```

The adstock value at time *t* depends only on media at times ≤ *t*. So an
assessment period's regressor draws on training-period *media*, which is
information genuinely available at prediction time, and never on future
media. No KPI information crosses the boundary at any point. The package tests
this invariant explicitly, precisely because the shortcut depends on it.

## Reading the result

`tuned$results` holds the whole grid, sorted from the best candidate down:

```{r}
head(tuned$results, 5)
```

The `results` grid is worth looking at rather than just taking `best`. If the
metric is nearly flat across a wide band of decay, the data does not identify
carryover tightly and a confident point estimate would be overstating things.

Two things in the output help with that. `std_err` is a jackknife standard
error of each candidate's metric over the splits, a measure of how noisy the
forecasts are. And `best_1se` applies the one-standard-error rule (Breiman et
al., 1984; Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, 2009): the *shortest* carryover
whose metric exceeds the best's by no more than one standard error of the
*paired difference* between the two. The comparison is paired because both
candidates face the same hard-to-forecast weeks, so the difference between
them is much less noisy than either metric on its own.

```{r}
rbind(best = tuned$best, one_se = tuned$best_1se)
```

Here both pick a decay of `r tuned$best_1se$decay`. When the two agree, the
data has spoken clearly. When they do not, the data cannot tell them apart.
The shorter carryover is the more conservative claim when the question is how
much credit a channel earns weeks after it ran, because a long carryover
flatters a channel; it is not conservative for every decision, since a
shorter carryover also lowers that channel's marginal return.

By default the metric is *pooled*: every out-of-sample forecast across all
splits is collected and `metric_fn` is evaluated once, so `rmse` is the root
mean squared forecast error. `aggregate = "mean"` averages a per-split metric
instead, which is the `tune` convention; with one-period assessment sets that
turns any RMSE into a mean absolute error, because the RMSE of a single point
is its absolute error.

`tune_carryover()` warns when the winner is pinned to the edge of the grid:

```{r}
narrow <- tune_carryover(spend, kpi, max_lags = Inf,
                         decays = seq(0.1, 0.5, by = 0.1))
narrow$best$decay
```

Here the truth is 0.7 and the grid stops at 0.5, so the optimum is outside it.
The warning is the signal to widen the grid rather than to believe the answer.

## The start of the series

Adstock starts from zero unless told otherwise, as if no media had ever run
before the first week. For a slow channel that understates the early weeks:

```{r}
steady <- rep(100, 8)
rbind(cold = adstock_geometric(steady, decay = 0.85),
      warm = adstock_geometric(steady, decay = 0.85,
                               state = adstock_steady_state(steady, 0.85)))
```

The cold start climbs towards the true level of 100 and is still short of it
after eight weeks; the warm start is there from the first week.
`adstock_steady_state()` seeds the filter as though the early average spend
had always been running, and `warm_start = TRUE` applies it to every
candidate in `tune_carryover()` and `tune_carryover_joint()`. Real pre-period
spend is better still when you have it: pass `adstock_state()` of it as the
`state` argument of `adstock_geometric()`.

## Sanity-check the answer against the data you have

```{r}
window <- effective_window(tuned$best$decay, coverage = 0.90)
window
```

The selected decay of `r round(tuned$best$decay, 2)` implies `r window` periods
before 90% of a burst's effect has played out. Compare that against the series
length: if the effective window approaches a large fraction of it, the
parameter is not identified by the data no matter how confident the
cross-validation looks. Here `r window` periods against `r n` is comfortable.

## Resampling schemes

Both schemes are forward-only; neither ever trains on data that follows what it
assesses. `"rolling_origin"` grows the training window one period at a time
and gives many splits; `"k_fold_forward"` uses a handful of contiguous forward
blocks and is cheaper on long series. Bergmeir and Benítez (2012) compare
evaluation on the last part of a series with cross-validation for time-series
predictors.

```{r}
rolling <- tune_carryover(spend, kpi, max_lags = Inf,
                          decays = seq(0.5, 0.9, by = 0.1),
                          scheme = "rolling_origin")
kfold <- tune_carryover(spend, kpi, max_lags = Inf,
                        decays = seq(0.5, 0.9, by = 0.1),
                        scheme = "k_fold_forward", k = 5)
c(rolling = rolling$best$decay, k_fold = kfold$best$decay)
```

Here the rolling-origin search picks `r rolling$best$decay` and the
forward-block search `r kfold$best$decay`.

## A correct objective is not the same as an easy problem

Everything above uses a single channel with no confounders. Real data is not
like that, and it is worth seeing how much harder it gets before trusting a
number.

`mm_weekly` has five mildly correlated, flighted channels (bought in bursts,
with weeks of no spend between them), a price term, a trend and seasonality,
and three years of weekly observations per geography. Here is what tuning
each channel's decay one at a time against north's raw revenue gives:

```{r}
data(mm_weekly)
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
truth_params <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")
grid <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.05)

channels <- names(truth_params$decay)

one_at_a_time <- vapply(channels, function(ch) {
  suppressWarnings(tune_carryover(north[[ch]], north$revenue,
                                  max_lags = Inf, decays = grid))$best$decay
}, numeric(1))

rbind(true = truth_params$decay[channels], recovered = one_at_a_time)
```

Some are close, some are badly off. Nothing is wrong with the objective, which
recovered every planted decay earlier. The problem is the *model* it is being
evaluated against: a univariate regression of revenue on one adstocked
channel, with no controls and no saturation. That model attributes the trend,
the price effect, seasonality and the other four channels' work to whichever
channel it is currently looking at, and the carryover that best predicts under
those conditions is not the true one.

Residualising the KPI against the controls first helps, but not enough:

```{r}
base <- lm(revenue ~ seq_len(nrow(north)) + price + seasonality + holiday,
           data = north)

residualised <- vapply(channels, function(ch) {
  suppressWarnings(tune_carryover(north[[ch]], residuals(base),
                                  max_lags = Inf, decays = grid))$best$decay
}, numeric(1))

rbind(true = truth_params$decay[channels],
      raw_kpi = one_at_a_time,
      residualised = residualised)
```

Residualising this way also lets future KPI values in, because the controls'
coefficients are estimated on the whole series, every split's assessment
period included; the `controls` argument of `tune_carryover()` fits them
inside each training window instead. Either way, carryover is not separable
from the rest of the specification, so tuning it one channel at a time against
a model you do not intend to fit answers a question you did not ask.

## Tuning every channel at once

`tune_carryover_joint()` puts all five channels and the controls into one
model and chooses each channel's decay with the others' effects accounted for.
It searches by coordinate descent, one channel at a time with the others held
fixed, repeating until nothing moves, so it costs a few sweeps of the
one-channel grid rather than the full five-dimensional grid:

```{r}
controls <- data.frame(week = seq_len(nrow(north)), price = north$price,
                       seasonality = north$seasonality,
                       holiday = north$holiday)

joint <- tune_carryover_joint(north[channels], north$revenue,
                              controls = controls, decays = grid)
joint

comparison <- rbind(true = truth_params$decay[channels],
                    one_at_a_time = one_at_a_time,
                    residualised = residualised,
                    joint = joint$best$decay,
                    joint_1se = joint$best_1se$decay)
comparison

# Mean absolute distance from the true decays
miss <- rowMeans(abs(sweep(comparison[-1, ], 2, comparison["true", ])))
round(miss, 2)
```

The joint search lands closer to the truth than tuning one channel at a time
(`r round(miss[["joint"]], 2)` against `r round(miss[["one_at_a_time"]], 2)` on
average) and matches residualising (`r round(miss[["residualised"]], 2)`), but
it is not uniformly better: for search it picks
`r comparison["joint", "search"]` against a truth of
`r comparison["true", "search"]`. The profiles show where the doubt lies:

```{r fig.height = 5.5}
plot(joint, truth = truth_params$decay)
```

Search's profile barely moves across most of the grid and rises only at the
longest carryovers: the data cannot tell the selected search half-life of
`r round(joint$best$half_life[joint$best$channel == "search"], 1)` weeks from
one of a fraction of a week, and that flatness is itself the finding, which a
point estimate without the profile would hide. The one-standard-error choices
(`decay_1se`, made channel by channel with the rule from *Reading the result*)
fall to the bottom of the grid for search, social and display. For search that
is near the truth; for social and display, whose true decays are
`r comparison["true", "social"]` and `r comparison["true", "display"]`, it is
not. A one-SE choice at the edge of the grid says the data cannot rule out a
short carryover, not that the carryover is short. The printed result also
reports the cross-validated error of the one-SE set as a whole
(`r round(joint$best_1se_metric)` against `r round(joint$metric)`),
which is worse than the best set's because each channel's choice was made with
the others held at their best.

The model here is still linear in adstocked media, with no saturation, so it
is not the model the data came from. For carryover tuned jointly with
saturation and a model penalty, use the recipe steps in
`vignette("tidymodels")`.
